cards.title: The Observability Tool Decision Framework
cards.teaser: The observability market is large, fast-moving, and full of vendors with overlapping claims. Evaluating tools by the problem they solve — not by feature lists or marketing — is the only framework that survives the churn. The right tool for a team of five running a monolith is not the right tool for a platform team managing 200 microservices.

runs.text: Observability tooling in 2026 spans fully managed SaaS platforms, self-hosted open-source systems, and a growing middle ground of open-source tools with commercial managed tiers. Vendor consolidation is real: Datadog acquired several niche players, Grafana Labs built a full OSS stack, Splunk was acquired by Cisco, and New Relic went through a leveraged buyout and privatization. The landscape will look different again in six months.
A decision framework that survives tool cycles evaluates candidates on five axes:

items.text: Signal coverage.
Does the tool handle all three pillars — logs, metrics, traces — or is it specialist? Specialist tools go deeper; all-in-one tools reduce the number of systems to operate and correlate across.
Cardinality model.

How does the tool handle high-cardinality data? Prometheus is architecturally cardinality-constrained. Honeycomb and Grafana Tempo are cardinality-tolerant. This is not a configuration choice — it is a fundamental architectural difference.
Ingest and query cost model.

Managed vendors typically charge on ingest volume, data retention, or seat count. OSS tools shift cost to infrastructure and operational effort. Neither is free — the question is which cost structure fits your scale and team.
Vendor lock-in surface.

Which behaviors are expressed in proprietary query languages, proprietary agents, or proprietary data formats? OpenTelemetry instrumentation is portable; vendor-specific SDKs are not. The lock-in you accept must be deliberate.
Operational burden.

A managed SaaS tool eliminates infrastructure operations at the cost of vendor dependency and ongoing subscription spend. A self-hosted OSS stack eliminates subscription cost at the cost of engineering time to operate, scale, and upgrade.

runs.text: This chapter frames what to evaluate, not what to deploy. Specific tool versions, pricing tiers, and feature parity shift every quarter. Apply these evaluation patterns to the current state of the tools you are comparing — do not treat any specific capability claim here as a guarantee about what a vendor ships today.

Evaluate observability tools on the problems they solve: signal coverage, cardinality tolerance, cost model, lock-in surface, and operational burden. Feature lists change quarterly; these axes stay stable.

cards.title: Prometheus — The Cloud-Native Metrics Default
cards.teaser: Prometheus is the de facto standard for metrics collection in cloud-native environments. Its pull-based scraping model, multi-dimensional data model, and PromQL query language are widely understood and deeply integrated into the Kubernetes ecosystem. The constraint is that it was not designed for long-term storage or global query at scale — that is a problem solved by the tooling built on top of it.

runs.text: Prometheus, originally developed at SoundCloud and donated to the CNCF in 2016 (graduated 2018), works by
scraping

HTTP endpoints that expose metrics in Prometheus text format. Services declare what metrics they export; Prometheus polls them on a configured interval. This pull model contrasts with push-based approaches (StatsD, InfluxDB line protocol) — the pull model makes it easy to detect when a scrape target disappears.
The data model is multi-dimensional: every metric is identified by a name and a set of key-value labels.
http_requests_total{method="POST", status="500"}
and
http_requests_total{method="GET", status="200"}
are distinct time series. PromQL aggregates and filters across labels, enabling flexible dashboards and alerts without pre-aggregating dimensions at ingest time.
What Prometheus does well:

items.text: Kubernetes-native.

The kube-state-metrics exporter, the Prometheus Operator, and the OpenTelemetry Collector's Prometheus exporter make scraping Kubernetes workloads near-zero configuration. Kubernetes itself exports metrics in Prometheus format.
Alerting with Alertmanager.
PromQL expressions define alert conditions. Alertmanager handles deduplication, grouping, inhibition, and routing to PagerDuty, Slack, email, and other receivers.
Exporter ecosystem.
Hundreds of exporters translate non-Prometheus metrics sources (databases, hardware, cloud APIs, network devices) into scrapeable endpoints. The ecosystem breadth is a genuine competitive advantage.

runs.text: Architectural constraints that matter:

items.text: Cardinality ceiling.

Prometheus stores every label combination as a separate time series in memory. A label with high cardinality — user ID, request ID, container ID — can create millions of series and exhaust memory. Cardinality is a first-class operational concern.
Local storage only.

Default Prometheus stores data on local disk with a configurable retention window (default 15 days). It has no built-in replication or multi-region querying. Long-term storage requires remote write to an external backend — this is where Cortex, Mimir, Thanos, and VictoriaMetrics come in.
Single point of failure.
A single Prometheus instance is a single point of failure. High-availability deployments run redundant scrapers and accept duplicate data, requiring deduplication at query time.

runs.text: Prometheus is the cloud-native metrics standard: it scrapes HTTP endpoints, stores multi-dimensional time series, and queries them with PromQL. Its limits are cardinality (too many label combinations OOM the server) and storage (it only keeps data locally for days, not months).

cards.title: Long-Term Prometheus Storage — Cortex, Mimir, Thanos, VictoriaMetrics
cards.teaser: Prometheus local storage does not scale past a single node and retains data for days, not months. Four major backends solve this: Cortex (the original multi-tenant remote-write backend), Mimir (Cortex's Grafana Labs fork), Thanos (sidecar-based object storage), and VictoriaMetrics (a high-performance alternative). Each makes different tradeoffs on architecture, complexity, and operational model.

runs.text: When you need metrics retention beyond Prometheus's local window, or need to query metrics across multiple Prometheus instances, you need a long-term storage backend. The four dominant options are:

items.text: Thanos.

A sidecar process runs alongside each Prometheus instance and uploads completed TSDB blocks to object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob). A query layer federates queries across all sidecars and the object store. Thanos is additive — you keep existing Prometheus instances and bolt long-term storage on top. Operational complexity is distributed across many components (Sidecar, Querier, Store Gateway, Compactor, Ruler).
Cortex.

The original CNCF project (graduated) for scalable, multi-tenant Prometheus storage. Services write via remote_write; Cortex ingests, indexes, and stores to object storage. Its microservices architecture (Distributor, Ingester, Querier, Compactor, Ruler, Alertmanager) allows independent horizontal scaling. Cortex is operationally complex but battle-tested at cloud-provider scale.
Grafana Mimir.

Grafana Labs forked Cortex in 2022, simplifying the deployment model and adding performance improvements. Mimir uses the same remote_write ingest model but reduces component count and improves query performance. Grafana Cloud is built on Mimir. If you are evaluating a self-hosted scalable Prometheus backend today, Mimir is generally the starting point over Cortex.
VictoriaMetrics.

A high-performance metrics storage engine with Prometheus compatibility. It accepts remote_write, exposes a Prometheus-compatible API, and runs as a single binary (or as a cluster). VictoriaMetrics uses significantly less disk and memory than Prometheus or Cortex for the same series count and is operationally simpler than Cortex or Thanos. The tradeoff is that it is not a CNCF project and has less ecosystem integration than Thanos or Mimir.

runs.text: Choosing between them:

items.text: Already running Prometheus, want minimal change:
Thanos is the least invasive — add sidecars, add object storage, keep existing Prometheus instances.
Want a scalable backend with managed-tier option:
Mimir has a Grafana Cloud managed tier; self-hosted is well-documented.
Want the lowest operational overhead and resource footprint:
VictoriaMetrics single-binary is operationally simplest and resource-efficient.
Need multi-tenancy at enterprise scale:
Cortex and Mimir both support strong multi-tenancy with tenant isolation; VictoriaMetrics cluster supports tenancy but less granularly.

runs.text: Prometheus alone only keeps data for days on a single node. Thanos bolts object storage onto existing Prometheus servers. Cortex and its Grafana fork Mimir are scalable remote-write backends with multi-tenancy. VictoriaMetrics is a leaner alternative that is easier to operate. Pick based on existing investment and operational capacity.

cards.title: Grafana — The Visualization and Dashboarding Layer
cards.teaser: Grafana is the dominant open-source visualization platform for observability data. It is datasource-agnostic — the same Grafana instance can query Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs, and Tempo for traces, correlating across signal types from a single UI. Understanding Grafana as the query-and-visualization layer, separate from its storage backends, is the architectural insight.

runs.text: Grafana (open-sourced in 2014, developed by Grafana Labs) began as a metrics visualization tool for Graphite and Prometheus. It has since expanded to a general observability frontend supporting over 50 datasource plugins — Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, Elasticsearch, Datadog, InfluxDB, PostgreSQL, and many more.
What the Grafana architecture gives you:

items.text: Unified observability correlation.

Grafana Explore lets engineers switch from a metric spike to the correlated logs (via Loki) to the correlated traces (via Tempo) without changing tools. Trace-to-logs and metrics-to-traces links are configured as datasource correlations. This cross-signal navigation is one of Grafana's genuine differentiators.
Dashboards as code.

Grafana dashboards are JSON documents. They can be stored in Git and deployed via Grafana's provisioning system or the Grafana Operator for Kubernetes. The Grafonnet library (Jsonnet) and Grafana's native dashboard-as-code tooling provide version-controlled, reviewable dashboard management.
Grafana Alerting.

Grafana ships a unified alerting engine that queries any datasource — not just Prometheus. Alert rules are written in PromQL, LogQL, or datasource-native query languages; routing and notification policies are managed in the Grafana UI, replacing or supplementing Prometheus Alertmanager.
Grafana Cloud.

Grafana Labs operates a fully managed cloud tier that bundles Grafana, Mimir (metrics), Loki (logs), Tempo (traces), and k6 (load testing) under one subscription. This is the path from the OSS LGTM stack to a managed offering without changing tooling or query languages.

runs.text: Grafana is not a storage backend — it is a query and visualization layer. Do not conflate Grafana with Prometheus; you can run Grafana without Prometheus (pointing at any datasource) and you can run Prometheus without Grafana (using the Prometheus expression browser or Alertmanager UI). The LGTM stack (Loki + Grafana + Tempo + Mimir) is the Grafana Labs open-source full-stack answer to a managed observability platform.

Grafana is a datasource-agnostic visualization layer. It queries Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs, and Tempo for traces, and lets you correlate across signal types in one UI. It does not store anything — that is what the backends it connects to are for.

cards.title: Loki — Log Aggregation with LogQL
cards.teaser: Grafana Loki is a horizontally scalable log aggregation system designed around the principle that logs should be indexed like Prometheus metrics — by labels, not by content. It does not build an inverted text index over log content, which makes it cheaper to operate than Elasticsearch at the cost of full-text search performance.

runs.text: Loki (open-sourced by Grafana Labs in 2018) takes a deliberate architectural position: index only the metadata labels attached to log streams, not the log content itself. Log content is compressed and stored as chunks in object storage. At query time, Loki filters candidate chunks by label, then applies a log pattern filter over the raw content. This is fundamentally different from Elasticsearch's approach of indexing every field.
The architectural implications:

items.text: Lower ingest cost.

No per-field indexing at ingest means significantly lower CPU, memory, and storage overhead compared to a full-text index. For high-volume log streams where you mostly query by service name, environment, and pod name, Loki's cost profile is substantially lower than Elasticsearch.
LogQL.
Loki's query language is deliberately modeled on PromQL. A developer who can write PromQL can read LogQL. Log stream selectors use the same label syntax:
{app="api", env="prod"}
. Log pipeline expressions (filter, pattern extract, metric extraction) are appended as pipeline stages. Loki log queries can be converted into metric queries for alerting.
Grafana integration.

Loki is the log backend in Grafana's LGTM stack. Trace-to-log correlation (clicking a Tempo trace span and seeing the correlated Loki log lines) works out of the box when both are configured as Grafana datasources.
Promtail and the OTel Collector.

Promtail is Loki's purpose-built agent, running as a DaemonSet in Kubernetes and tailing container logs. The OpenTelemetry Collector also ships a Loki exporter, providing an OTel-native path to Loki ingest.

runs.text: Where Loki is a poor fit:

items.text: Ad-hoc full-text search over arbitrary fields.

If the primary use case is security log analysis with complex multi-field searches, Elasticsearch or Splunk will outperform Loki significantly. Loki's label model requires knowing which dimensions to label at ingest time.
Cardinality in labels.

Like Prometheus, Loki's label index grows with cardinality. High-cardinality labels (user ID in a label, trace ID as a label) will degrade query performance and increase storage overhead for the label index.

runs.text: Loki indexes log metadata labels (like Prometheus), not log content. This makes it cheap to operate at high ingest volume but slower than Elasticsearch for ad-hoc full-text searches. If you are already on the Grafana + Prometheus stack, Loki is the natural log backend.

cards.title: Tempo — Grafana's Distributed Tracing Backend
cards.teaser: Grafana Tempo is a high-scale distributed tracing backend that stores traces in object storage and retrieves them by trace ID. It deliberately avoids building a search index over trace attributes, trading search flexibility for very low storage cost — making it practical to store 100% of traces rather than sampling down to reduce index cost.

runs.text: Tempo (open-sourced by Grafana Labs in 2020) solves a specific problem in distributed tracing: most tracing backends (Jaeger, Zipkin, early Elasticsearch-backed systems) store traces in a searchable index that becomes expensive at high ingest rates, forcing teams to sample aggressively — often 1-5% of traces.
Tempo's architectural position:

items.text: Object storage backend.

Traces are written directly to object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) as Parquet files. The primary index is the trace ID. Retrieval by trace ID is fast. Attribute-level search across all traces is a separate, heavier operation (Tempo's TraceQL supports it but at higher query cost).
High sample rate by design.

Because object storage is cheap relative to indexed search storage, Tempo makes it economically practical to store 100% of traces. The tail sampling decision (which traces to keep based on outcome) happens upstream in the OTel Collector or Grafana Alloy; Tempo itself stores whatever it receives.
TraceQL.
Tempo's native query language allows searching for traces by span attributes, duration, status, and nested conditions.
{ .http.status_code = 500 && duration > 2s }
finds traces containing an HTTP 500 span longer than 2 seconds. TraceQL queries scan Parquet files — powerful but not instant.
Grafana integration.

Tempo is the T in LGTM. Grafana datasource correlations link Prometheus exemplars (which embed trace IDs in metric samples) to Tempo, and link Tempo spans to Loki log lines. The cross-pillar navigation is native.

runs.text: Tempo accepts OTLP, Jaeger, Zipkin, and OpenCensus formats, making it a drop-in backend for applications already instrumented with OpenTelemetry or Jaeger clients. No re-instrumentation is required to switch the storage backend to Tempo.

Tempo stores traces in object storage indexed only by trace ID. This makes it very cheap — you can store 100% of traces instead of sampling aggressively. The tradeoff is that searching traces by attribute is slower than in Elasticsearch-backed tracers.

cards.title: Jaeger — Distributed Tracing from Uber
cards.teaser: Jaeger is a CNCF-graduated distributed tracing system originally developed at Uber. It predates OpenTelemetry and established the concepts of client libraries, a collector, a query service, and a storage backend. Jaeger has evolved to embrace OTel as its primary instrumentation path, and most new deployments use the OpenTelemetry Collector to forward traces to Jaeger's backend.

runs.text: Jaeger was open-sourced by Uber in 2017, inspired by Google Dapper and Twitter Zipkin, and became a CNCF project the same year (graduated 2019). It introduced a clear reference architecture: client-side instrumentation, a collector that receives spans and writes to storage, a query service for retrieval, and a web UI for visualization.
Where Jaeger fits today:

items.text: OTel-first instrumentation.

The Jaeger project actively recommends using OpenTelemetry SDKs for instrumentation and the OTel Collector to forward traces to Jaeger. Jaeger's own client libraries (jaeger-client-go, jaeger-client-java) are in maintenance mode. New deployments should use OTel SDKs.
Pluggable storage backends.

Jaeger supports Cassandra, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Kafka (as a buffer), and Badger (local) as storage backends. The choice of storage backend determines Jaeger's scalability characteristics — Elasticsearch is the most common production choice and supports attribute-level search.
Service dependency graph.

Jaeger's UI generates service dependency graphs from trace data, showing call relationships between services. This topology view is useful for understanding microservice dependencies during incidents.
Jaeger v2 (OTEL-native).

Jaeger v2 rearchitects the collector as an OTel Collector distribution, accepting OTLP natively. This aligns Jaeger's ingest path with the broader OTel ecosystem while retaining the Jaeger query and UI layer.

runs.text: Jaeger vs Tempo: the key evaluation question is whether you need rich attribute-level search across all traces (Elasticsearch-backed Jaeger is stronger here) or low-cost storage with 100% trace retention (Tempo with object storage). Many teams run Tempo for cost reasons and accept TraceQL for attribute searches.

Jaeger is the CNCF tracing system from Uber. It has embraced OpenTelemetry as its instrumentation path and supports multiple storage backends. Use it when you need richer attribute-level trace search than Tempo's object-storage model provides.

cards.title: Datadog — Vendor-Managed All-in-One
cards.teaser: Datadog is the dominant commercial observability platform. It provides logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, alerts, synthetics, security monitoring, and profiling under one product with a unified data model and a single agent. The value is breadth, depth of integrations, and zero operational overhead. The cost is billing per host, per GB, per retention tier — and it escalates fast at scale.

runs.text: Datadog (founded 2010, IPO 2019) is the commercial reference implementation of the all-in-one observability platform. Its Agent runs on every host, collects metrics, logs, traces, and system profiles, and ships them to Datadog's SaaS backend. Engineers work in a single UI for all signal types. Alert rules, dashboards, and SLO tracking are in one product.
Genuine differentiators:

items.text: Integration depth.

Datadog ships hundreds of integrations — cloud provider APIs, databases, message queues, Kubernetes, serverless runtimes. The time from deploying the Agent to seeing meaningful dashboards is measured in minutes, not days.
APM and distributed tracing.
Datadog APM provides automatic instrumentation for Java, Python, Go, Ruby, Node.js, and .NET. Flame graphs, service maps, and trace-to-log correlation are polished and default-configured.
OTel ingest.

Datadog added native OTLP ingest — the Datadog Agent accepts OTLP traces and metrics directly. This is a strategic move acknowledging that OTel has won as the instrumentation standard. Teams can instrument with OTel SDKs and ship to Datadog without Datadog-specific client libraries.
Dashboards and notebooks.
Datadog's notebook product (combining narrative text, metric graphs, log queries, and trace visualizations) is a strong incident review and postmortem tool that has no direct OSS equivalent.

runs.text: The cost and lock-in reality:

items.text: Per-host billing.

Datadog charges per monitored host per month, with additional charges per GB of log ingest and per volume of custom metrics. Cost grows linearly with infrastructure size and can become the largest SaaS line item for organizations running hundreds of hosts.
Agent dependency.

Deep investment in Datadog APM auto-instrumentation and Datadog-specific dashboards creates switching cost. OTel ingest reduces instrumentation lock-in, but dashboard configuration and alert logic remain proprietary.

runs.text: Datadog is the all-in-one commercial observability platform: one agent, one SaaS backend, one UI for metrics, logs, traces, and alerts. It is the fastest path to full observability coverage. The cost scales with host count and data volume, and the switching cost grows with platform depth.

cards.title: Honeycomb — High-Cardinality Wide Events
cards.teaser: Honeycomb is the commercial platform that operationalized observability as Charity Majors and the Honeycomb team defined it — wide events with arbitrary high-cardinality fields, queried interactively to find the specific user, request, or deployment that explains an anomaly. It is architecturally incompatible with the pre-aggregated metrics mindset and represents a different philosophy, not a better metrics tool.

runs.text: Honeycomb (founded 2016) was built from a thesis: the right data structure for debugging production systems is a
wide event

— a single structured record containing every attribute relevant to one unit of work (an HTTP request, a database query, a message consumed). User ID, customer tier, feature flag state, query plan, upstream service response time — all in one row, 50-300 fields wide.
What this model enables:

items.text: Arbitrary cardinality.
Honeycomb stores raw events, not pre-aggregated time series. Querying by
user_id = "u_abc123"
is a first-class operation — not a cardinality explosion. This is the defining architectural difference from Prometheus-based systems, where high-cardinality labels are operationally dangerous.
BubbleUp.

Honeycomb's BubbleUp feature compares the attribute distribution of slow/errored events against the baseline distribution. It surfaces which field values are overrepresented in the slow tail — often identifying the exact customer segment, feature flag, or region responsible for degradation without manual hypothesis testing.
Dynamic sampling.

Honeycomb's Refinery proxy performs dynamic tail-based sampling, keeping 100% of error traces and interesting traces while sampling down the fast-path baseline. This preserves signal quality without paying full ingest cost for all traffic.
Strongly typed for traces.
Honeycomb traces are wide events at the span level — the span carries every attribute relevant to that unit of work. This aligns naturally with OpenTelemetry's span attribute model.

runs.text: Honeycomb is not a Prometheus replacement or a Grafana alternative. It occupies a different position: it is optimized for debugging unknown failures on production distributed systems using high-cardinality event data. Teams using Honeycomb still often run Prometheus + Grafana for infrastructure metrics dashboards. The tools serve different investigation workflows.

Honeycomb stores wide events — a single row per request with every attribute you might want to debug by, including high-cardinality fields like user ID. It lets you ask questions you did not anticipate. Prometheus aggregates data before storing it, making high-cardinality queries impossible by design.

cards.title: New Relic — Vendor-Managed APM
cards.teaser: New Relic is one of the oldest APM vendors, having defined application performance monitoring before the term observability existed. It has evolved from an agent-based APM platform to a full-stack observability product with a usage-based pricing model. Its trajectory — private equity acquisition, OpenTelemetry investment, unified data platform — is a case study in how legacy APM vendors are repositioning in an OTel-native world.

runs.text: New Relic (founded 2008) pioneered the SaaS APM model: install an agent, see your application's transaction traces and error rates in a dashboard within minutes. For years it competed primarily with AppDynamics and Dynatrace in the enterprise APM market.
Where New Relic differentiates today:

items.text: New Relic Database (NRDB).

New Relic stores all telemetry — metrics, events, logs, traces — in a unified columnar data store called NRDB. NRQL (New Relic Query Language) is a SQL-like query language that queries across all signal types. This unified store avoids the join-across-backends problem common in OSS stacks.
Usage-based pricing.

New Relic shifted from per-host billing to per-GB ingest pricing. This aligns cost with actual data volume, which benefits teams running many small services but can surprise teams with high log ingest rates.
OpenTelemetry investment.

New Relic is an OpenTelemetry project contributor and supports OTLP ingest natively. New Relic's agent libraries are being repositioned as optional enrichment on top of OTel instrumentation, not as the required instrumentation path.
Change tracking and deployments.

New Relic's Change Tracking feature marks deployment events in time series, correlating metric behavior changes with deploys. This is useful context when investigating latency regressions following a code push.

runs.text: The market context: New Relic went private in 2023 following a leveraged buyout by Francisco Partners and TPG. The acquisition introduced organizational uncertainty. When evaluating New Relic today, assess product roadmap continuity alongside technical capability — the ownership structure affects long-term vendor stability.

New Relic is a full-stack observability SaaS that stores all signals — metrics, logs, traces, events — in one queryable store (NRDB). It went private in 2023 and has pivoted to OTel-native instrumentation. It competes with Datadog on breadth, with usage-based pricing rather than per-host billing.

cards.title: Splunk — Enterprise Logs and Observability
cards.teaser: Splunk built its business on log search and analytics at enterprise scale. Its Search Processing Language (SPL), data pipeline, and security analytics capabilities established it as the reference platform for large organizations with compliance-heavy log management requirements. Cisco acquired Splunk in 2024, adding enterprise network telemetry to its observability ambitions.

runs.text: Splunk (founded 2003, IPO 2012) solved a real problem: enterprise IT operations teams needed to search logs from thousands of disparate systems — network devices, Windows event logs, UNIX syslogs, application logs — in a single tool. SPL (Search Processing Language) became the query lingua franca for operations teams in large enterprises. Splunk's value was not just the search engine; it was the ecosystem of technology add-ons that normalized heterogeneous log formats.
What Splunk does well:

items.text: SPL expressiveness.

SPL is a pipeline query language capable of extracting fields, joining datasets, computing statistics, and generating visualizations from raw log data. Its flexibility exceeds LogQL or Datadog's log query language for complex analytical workloads.
Security and SIEM.

Splunk Enterprise Security is one of the leading SIEM products. Organizations that use Splunk for security monitoring often extend it for observability to avoid maintaining separate log pipelines. The security analytics capability is a genuine differentiator.
Data ingestion breadth.

Splunk's technology add-on ecosystem supports data normalization from hundreds of source types. For organizations with complex on-premises infrastructure and heterogeneous log sources, this ecosystem reduces normalization work.

runs.text: The strategic context — Cisco acquisition:

items.text: Cisco completed its acquisition of Splunk in March 2024 for $28 billion.

The strategic rationale combines Splunk's observability and SIEM capabilities with Cisco's network telemetry and ThousandEyes infrastructure. The product roadmap post-acquisition is still emerging. Organizations evaluating Splunk for new deployments should assess the combined Cisco-Splunk roadmap, not the pre-acquisition trajectory.
Cost.

Splunk's per-GB ingest pricing has historically been the highest in the market for comparable functionality. This has driven the growth of alternatives (OpenSearch, Loki, Cribl as a data pipeline before Splunk ingest) specifically positioned as Splunk cost-reduction tools.

runs.text: Splunk is the enterprise log search and analytics platform, dominant in security operations (SIEM) and operations teams managing heterogeneous infrastructure. Cisco acquired it in 2024. Its query language (SPL) is powerful; its per-GB ingest pricing is expensive, which has driven a cottage industry of Splunk cost-reduction tooling.

cards.title: Elastic Stack (ELK) — Logs and Beyond
cards.teaser: The Elastic Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana — ELK) is the dominant open-source log management and search platform. Elasticsearch's inverted-text-index model enables full-text search over arbitrary fields that Loki's label-only index does not support. The stack has expanded from log management to metrics (via Metricbeat and Elastic APM) and traces (via Elastic APM agent and OTel support), becoming a full-stack observability competitor.

runs.text: Elasticsearch (open-sourced 2010, built on Apache Lucene) became the de facto backend for log aggregation when combined with Logstash (ingest pipeline) and Kibana (visualization). The ELK stack achieved widespread adoption because it was open source, horizontally scalable, and provided full-text search over structured and unstructured log data.
The Elastic Stack today:

items.text: Elasticsearch as the core.

Elasticsearch indexes every field of every document at ingest. This enables arbitrary full-text searches, range queries, and aggregations over any logged field — query latency, user ID, SQL query text, error message substring — without pre-declaring dimensions. This is fundamentally more flexible than Loki's label-only model.
Elastic APM.

Elastic APM provides distributed tracing and application performance monitoring, storing traces in Elasticsearch alongside logs. Kibana APM correlates traces with log lines using trace ID, providing a unified view without multiple backends.
OpenTelemetry support.

Elastic ships an OTel Collector distribution and accepts OTLP over GRPC. Elastic APM agents and OTel SDKs can coexist; teams migrating to OTel instrumentation can continue sending data to Elasticsearch without changing storage or visualization.
Operational cost.

Indexing every field is expensive. An Elasticsearch cluster ingesting high-volume application logs requires significantly more disk, CPU, and memory than a Loki deployment handling the same log volume. Hot-warm-cold tier architecture (newer, more expensive hardware for recent data; cheaper nodes for older data) is standard for production Elasticsearch at scale.

runs.text: Licensing note: Elastic changed Elasticsearch's license to SSPL in 2021, prompting AWS to fork it as OpenSearch (Apache 2.0). Organizations evaluating an Elasticsearch deployment should assess whether SSPL compatibility matters for their use case. OpenSearch maintains feature parity for most observability workloads.

Elasticsearch indexes every field of every log document, enabling full-text search over anything you log. That flexibility costs more compute and storage than Loki. ELK is the right choice when you need ad-hoc search over arbitrary log fields; Loki is better when you primarily filter by known metadata labels.

cards.title: AIOps — Machine Learning Over Telemetry
cards.teaser: AIOps applies machine learning to observability telemetry to automate pattern detection, anomaly surfacing, and root-cause hints. The promise is reducing alert noise, detecting novel failures faster, and accelerating incident investigation. The reality is that ML over time-series telemetry is genuinely useful for specific problems and overpromised for others — distinguishing the two is the operational skill.

runs.text: AIOps (AI for IT Operations, a term from Gartner) applies machine learning and statistical models to the streams of logs, metrics, and traces that observability systems produce. It is not a product category in itself — it is a capability now embedded in most major observability platforms (Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, Splunk) and several standalone products.
Where AIOps delivers real value:

items.text: Anomaly detection on metrics.

Seasonal and trend-aware anomaly detection identifies metric deviations that threshold-based alerts cannot catch. A service that has higher traffic on weekday mornings needs a dynamic baseline, not a static threshold. ML models that learn seasonality reduce false positives from traffic-correlated metric changes.
Alert correlation and noise reduction.

During an incident, tens or hundreds of alerts fire simultaneously from a single root cause. AIOps correlation engines group related alerts, identify the probable root event, and suppress downstream symptoms. This is one of the highest-value AIOps applications — alert fatigue is a real problem and automatic grouping has measurable impact.
Log clustering.

Grouping similar log lines by semantic pattern (rather than exact string match) reduces the noise of high-volume log streams. ML-based log parsing can identify new error patterns without manual rule authoring.
Root-cause hints.

Tools like Datadog Watchdog, Dynatrace Davis, and New Relic AI correlate metric, log, and trace signals to surface probable root causes. These are investigative hints, not verdicts — the human on-call validates and acts.

runs.text: Where AIOps overpromises:

items.text: Fully automated remediation.
Auto-remediation on AI-detected anomalies in production is high-risk without well-bounded failure domains. ML models make false positives; automated actions on false positives can escalate incidents.
New system cold start.
ML-based anomaly detection requires sufficient historical data to build a baseline. A new system with days of data will generate noisy anomalies until the model has learned normal behavior.

runs.text: AIOps uses machine learning on your telemetry to detect anomalies, correlate related alerts, and surface root-cause hints. It genuinely reduces alert noise and speeds up investigation. It does not replace human judgment for remediation decisions — it provides better inputs to the human making the call.

cards.title: Vendor Lock-in vs OpenTelemetry — The Strategic Calculus
cards.teaser: The central strategic tension in observability tooling is vendor lock-in versus the flexibility of OTel-native instrumentation. Choosing a vendor-managed platform buys operational simplicity and feature richness at the cost of portability. Investing in OpenTelemetry as the instrumentation layer preserves backend flexibility at the cost of more architecture decisions. The calculus is not the same for every team.

runs.text: OpenTelemetry's core promise is separating
instrumentation
from
backend

. Instrument once with OTel SDKs; route telemetry to any backend via the OTel Collector. Swap backends — or run multiple simultaneously — by reconfiguring the Collector, not by re-instrumenting every service.
Lock-in layers in observability, from shallow to deep:

items.text: Instrumentation (shallow with OTel).

OTel SDK instrumentation is vendor-neutral. If you instrument with OTel, switching the backend does not require touching application code. If you instrument with Datadog's dd-trace libraries or New Relic agents, instrumentation is the lock-in.
Agent and Collector configuration (medium).
Pipeline configuration in the OTel Collector is portable across backends. Vendor-specific agent configurations (Datadog Agent, New Relic Infrastructure Agent) are proprietary and do not translate.
Query language (deep).

Dashboards and alert rules written in PromQL are portable across Prometheus, Mimir, Thanos, and VictoriaMetrics. Rules written in NRQL, SPL, or Datadog's query language are not portable. This is often the deepest lock-in — organizations with hundreds of dashboards and alert rules in a proprietary query language face a significant migration cost.
Platform features (deepest).
Datadog Watchdog, Honeycomb BubbleUp, Dynatrace Davis — these AI-driven investigative tools have no direct equivalents elsewhere. Workflows that depend on them are fully platform-specific.

runs.text: The practical recommendation:

items.text: Always use OTel SDKs for new instrumentation.

Vendor-specific instrumentation libraries are in retreat — every major vendor now accepts OTLP. There is no cost to instrumenting with OTel and routing to a vendor; there is a real cost to instrumenting with vendor SDKs and later wanting to switch.
Accept query language lock-in deliberately.

PromQL has the most portable backend ecosystem. Investing in PromQL dashboards and alerts is the lowest-lock-in choice for metrics. For logs and traces, assess the migration cost of proprietary query languages before committing.
Evaluate platform features as deliberate lock-in.
The best vendor-specific features (Honeycomb BubbleUp, Datadog APM flame graphs) may justify the lock-in. Evaluate whether the value exchanged is worth the switching cost — just do it consciously.

runs.text: The most durable observability investment is OTel-native instrumentation throughout your services, with a well-configured OTel Collector pipeline that could route to a different backend by changing configuration. The backend can be swapped; re-instrumenting hundreds of services cannot be undone cheaply.

Use OTel SDKs for instrumentation — it keeps you portable across backends. Accept lock-in at the query language and platform feature layer only when the value is worth the switching cost. The instrumentation layer is the hardest to redo; the backend is the easiest to swap.

cards.title: OSS vs Vendor-Managed — The Decision Framework
cards.teaser: The choice between self-hosted open-source observability and vendor-managed SaaS is not a technical question — it is an organizational capacity question. Both paths can produce excellent observability. The path that fails is the one chosen for the wrong reasons: OSS to save money without accounting for operational cost, or SaaS to avoid decisions without modeling billing at scale.

runs.text: The OSS observability stack (Prometheus + Mimir + Loki + Tempo + Grafana) and the vendor-managed options (Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic, Grafana Cloud) represent two different organizational bets. Both are used successfully at scale. The question is which bet fits your team.

items.text: Choose OSS self-hosted when:

you have infrastructure engineering capacity to operate the stack; data sovereignty or compliance requirements prohibit third-party data processors; ingest volume makes vendor billing prohibitive; or you have existing Kubernetes platform investment that absorbs the operational overhead.
Choose vendor-managed when:

your team lacks infrastructure engineering capacity; time-to-value matters more than long-term cost optimization; you need the breadth of integrations that only a well-funded commercial product ships; or you want to defer architecture decisions until you understand your observability needs better.
Choose Grafana Cloud (OSS tooling, managed tier) when:

you want to use OTel instrumentation and PromQL/LogQL without managing the storage backends; you may migrate to self-hosted Mimir/Loki/Tempo later; or you want a lower cost ceiling than Datadog at high ingest volume.

runs.text: The comparison that matters most — total cost at your scale:

items.text: Vendor-managed cost.

Model ingest volume, host count, log retention, and seat count against vendor pricing. Datadog and Splunk costs at 500+ hosts with 30-day log retention are often the largest SaaS line items. The sticker price is never the actual bill.
Self-hosted cost.

Cloud compute and storage for the observability stack, plus engineering time to deploy, upgrade, scale, and maintain. Two platform engineers spending 20% of their time on observability infrastructure is a real cost, not a free alternative.
Hybrid model.

Many organizations run vendor-managed for metrics and traces (Datadog APM) while self-hosting for logs (Loki or Elasticsearch) where ingest volume makes vendor pricing untenable. The signal that makes the most economic sense on a managed tier is not the same for every team.

runs.text: The most common observability mistake is choosing OSS to save money and then discovering the operational cost was not accounted for — resulting in a degraded, under-maintained observability stack. The second most common mistake is choosing a vendor and discovering the bill at scale was not modeled. Do the math before you commit.

OSS observability is cheaper at scale if you have the engineering capacity to operate it. Vendor-managed is faster to value and eliminates ops burden at the cost of a large recurring bill. Many teams run both — vendor for some signals, self-hosted for others — based on where the economics tip.
